query: Consider the following context: High Entropy Alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) have been synthetized because they are promising materials to improve nanoscale performance. However, little theoretical study has been carried out regarding the thermal stability of HEA NPs. In that context, which method can be used for study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi HEA NPs as a function of size, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi HEA NPs can be studied as a function of size using in situ aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and melting of a surface layer
generation.predicted_outcome: Strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of a surface layer at high temperature
generation.baseline: Thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi HEA NPs at room temperature
generation.uncertainty: The exact thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi HEA NPs as a function of size is uncertain and requires further study

falsification_experiment.design: In situ STEM heating experiment with molecular dynamics simulations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant structural evolution is observed in the NPs at high temperature, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. NP Synthesis

Pulsed laser deposition has been widely used for the synthesis of bimetallic nanoalloys. [ [17] , [18] ] The fabrication method permits an alternating deposition of pure metals on the substrate to form nanoalloys of controlled size and composition, using a COMPex KrF excimer laser beam in a high vacuum chamber. The experimental conditions for the fabrication of sub‐10 nm AuCoCuNiPt NPs near the equiatomic composition were recently reported. [ [2] ] In the present study, the same HENA was directly synthetized on the SiN membrane of a heating MEMS chip commercialized by Protochips for in situ TEM investigations. A substrate temperature of 873 K, a laser frequency of 5 Hz, and a total nominal thickness of 4 nm measured prior to metal deposition were measured with a quartz crystal microbalance. Same HENA were also prepared on an ultra thin amorphous carbon film to acquire high‐quality TEM data of as‐grown NPs.
